edges.description: Remodeling of sinoatrial nodal tissue impairs propagation of pacemaker impulses to the atrial myocardium.

The same degenerative loss of pacemaker-cell automaticity that produces exit block also blunts the sinus rate response to exercise, so the heart rate fails to rise appropriately with metabolic demand.
Signaling dysregulation in sinoatrial pacemaker tissue can impair impulse generation or exit to atrial myocardium.
Dropped atrial activation and pauses slow the ventricular rate and can reduce end-organ perfusion.
Intermittent failure of sinoatrial impulses to reach the atrium drops atrial and hence ventricular activations, producing the slow rate recorded on the surface electrocardiogram.
Patients perceive the dropped beats and the post-pause escape or sinus beats that follow them as irregularity or a pounding sensation.
A pause long enough to drop cerebral perfusion below the autoregulatory threshold causes transient loss of consciousness.
Shorter or less severe reductions in cerebral perfusion produce the near-faint sensation without complete loss of consciousness.
Transient cerebral hypoperfusion during bradycardia or pauses is experienced as lightheadedness or vertigo.
Chronically inadequate cardiac output limits systemic oxygen delivery and is reported by patients as tiredness and reduced exercise tolerance.
Rate-slowing drugs depress sinoatrial automaticity and nodal conduction directly, and are the leading extrinsic and reversible cause of sinoatrial exit block in susceptible patients.

evidence.snippet: Electrocardiography findings include sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses or arrest, sinoatrial exit block, chronotropic incompetence, or alternating bradycardia and tachycardia (i.e., bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome).

nodes.description: Recurrent sinus pauses can slow ventricular rate enough to reduce cerebral and systemic perfusion.

evidence.snippet: Clinical symptoms result from the hypoperfusion of end organs.
The causes of sinus node dysfunction are intrinsic (e.g., degenerative idiopathic fibrosis, cardiac remodeling) or extrinsic (e.g., medications, metabolic abnormalities) to the sinoatrial node.

The patient's inability to reach a heart rate of at least 80% of their predicted maximum (220 beats per minute - age) may indicate chronotropic incompetence, which is present in 50% of patients with sinus node dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: First-line treatment for patients with confirmed sinus node dysfunction is permanent pacemaker placement with atrial-based pacing and limited ventricular pacing when necessary.
Other symptoms include palpitations, decreased physical activity tolerance, angina, muscular fatigue, or oliguria.
About 50% of patients present with cerebral hypoperfusion (e.g., syncope, presyncope, lightheadedness, cerebrovascular accident).
